title: Waypoint-OPD: Transferring RL-Induced Policy Shifts via Gated On-Policy Distillation

paper.title: Waypoint-OPD: Transferring RL-Induced Policy Shifts via Gated On-Policy Distillation Thanks: Corresponding author.
paper.abstract:
Abstract Policy-shift distillation reuses the difference between a teacher’s log probabilities before and after reinforcement learning (RL) as supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, this endpoint policy shift cannot reveal whether local
action preferences evolved consistently during teacher training. The same endpoint shift can result from early and late shifts that reinforce or partially cancel each other. We investigate whether agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts can guide selective transfer. We introduce Waypoint-guided On-Policy Distillation (Waypoint-OPD), which uses an intermediate teacher checkpoint from the same RL run to compare early and late shifts in relative action preferences at student-visited prefixes. We gate the endpoint shift according to the directional agreement between the early and late shifts, suppressing it when they point in opposing directions. Compared with endpoint-only transfer, our method requires only one additional frozen-teacher scoring pass. Using RL-trained Qwen3-4B teachers, we evaluate our method with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B as student models in mathematical and code reasoning. In all six domain–student settings, Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest domain-average score among the compared distillation methods. Ablations with the Qwen3-8B student show that removing or shuffling gates reduces mathematical reasoning performance. These results support the use of directional agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts to weight the endpoint shift during student training. Our code is available at https://github.com/hhhbxloveai/WaypointOPD .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning can improve language-model instruction following using rewards learned from human preferences ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and mathematical and code reasoning using verifiable rewards ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . The latter requires repeated generation, verification, and optimization of on-policy responses. Reusing a teacher’s RL improvements offers a way to share this training effort across target models. This raises the question: which local changes in the teacher’s policy should guide a student on its own generated trajectories? Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) trains the student to match the teacher’s token distributions on student-generated prefixes ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Its supervision remains tied to the teacher’s absolute policy and capability limitations. On-Policy Delta Distillation ( OPD 2 ) uses the change between a reasoning-tuned teacher and its base model, retaining token-level signals when the centered change agrees in sign with the centered standard distillation signal ( Heo et al., 2026 ) . Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) focuses on RL-induced improvements. It uses the log-probability ratio between pre-RL and post-RL teacher checkpoints as a dense implicit reward on student-generated states, transferring the teacher’s policy change without matching its absolute distribution ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . Both methods extract changes from a pair of teacher models, but neither directly measures whether consecutive changes during teacher RL point in compatible directions. The Initial-to-Final log-probability ratio captures only the change between the teacher’s policies before and after RL training. The same endpoint signal can arise from early and late policy changes that point in similar or opposing directions. Endpoint-only transfer cannot distinguish these cases. We hypothesize that agreement between the early and late changes provides evidence for deciding how much weight to assign an endpoint shift at a student-generated prefix. Building on this hypothesis, we propose Waypoint-OPD, which uses agreement between consecutive teacher shifts to gate the endpoint transfer signal. We retain three checkpoints from the same teacher RL run: Initial before RL, Waypoint at an intermediate RL step, and Final at the end of RL. At each student-generated prefix, we select its top- k k most probable next-token candidates. Over these candidates, we compare how the teacher’s relative preferences change from Initial to Waypoint and from Waypoint to Final. Their agreement gates the centered Initial-to-Final signal, retaining aligned changes and suppressing reversals. Waypoint thus supplies evidence for weighting the endpoint shift, which remains the transferred signal. Relative to endpoint-only transfer, this requires one additional frozen teacher scoring pass, with no new teacher training or verifier calls during student transfer. Our contributions are: • Temporal agreement as a criterion for selective transfer. We use the Waypoint checkpoint to assess temporal agreement at student-generated prefixes, revealing directional information unavailable from the endpoint pair alone. • Waypoint-guided gating of endpoint signals. We develop Waypoint-OPD, a dense on-policy objective that uses this agreement to weight the endpoint signal at each student-generated prefix, with one additional frozen teacher scoring pass. • Higher average performance across domains and model sizes. We evaluate Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) on mathematics and code. Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest recorded domain average among the evaluated baselines in all six settings (Figure 1 and Tables 1 and 2 ). Ablations on Qwen3-8B mathematical reasoning support the value of temporal gating (Table 3 ).

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We examine three questions: Q1. Does Waypoint-OPD improve transfer across math, code, and model scales? Q2. Does temporal consistency improve on endpoint transfer and Final-teacher imitation? Q3. How do gate assignment, mean normalization, and Waypoint position affect performance? Supplementary training-time and response-length analyses appear in Appendix H .

sections.heading: Teacher checkpoints and student models.
sections.text: For each domain, we use three checkpoints from the same Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) RL run: Initial ( π 0 \pi_{0} ) before RL, Waypoint ( π m \pi_{m} ) at RL step 600, and Final ( π 1 \pi_{1} ) at RL step 1200. Math and code teachers use non-thinking RL. All three checkpoints remain frozen during transfer. We train Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B students using the teacher’s RL-induced policy shifts. These students span three scales and dense and MoE architectures within one family with compatible tokenizers. The transfer objective does not require the teacher to outperform the student. We report all three teacher checkpoints and the Base students in the result tables to show pre-transfer performance.

sections.heading: Training and evaluation data.
sections.text: Math transfer uses DAPO-Math-17K prompts ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . We evaluate on seven benchmarks: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AIME 2026, HMMT February 2025, HMMT November 2025, HMMT February 2026, and AMC 2023. For each problem, mean@32 measures average correctness over 32 generated responses. Benchmark scores average these values over problems, and Avg. is the unweighted mean across benchmarks. Code transfer uses a Codeforces-derived prompt set. Evaluation uses the 378-problem MBPP+ set from EvalPlus ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , reporting both the original MBPP tests ( Austin et al., 2021 ) and the original plus additional tests (MBPP+), together with LiveCodeBench v4, v5, and v6 ( Jain et al., 2025 ) . We report mean@8 , which averages correctness over eight generated responses per problem and then over the problems in each benchmark. Code Avg. is the unweighted mean over these five evaluation scores. Within each benchmark, methods share prompt templates, decoding parameters, maximum generation lengths, and sample counts.

sections.heading: Student checkpoint selection.
sections.text: For both domains, we use AIME 2024 as the validation set and select each trained student’s checkpoint with the highest validation accuracy. All benchmark results for that student use this selected checkpoint.

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: We build on verl ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) and score the student’s top-16 token IDs with the three frozen teachers. The transfer objective combines the dense distillation reward with the student KL penalty. Answer graders are used only for evaluation. Implementation and training/evaluation configurations appear in Appendices B and C .

sections.heading: 4.2 Baselines and controls
sections.text: We compare against the Base student, standard on-policy distillation (OPD) from the Final teacher ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , OPD 2 with its sampled-token objective ( Heo et al., 2026 ) , and endpoint Direct-OPD using log ⁡ π 1 − log ⁡ π 0 \log\pi_{1}-\log\pi_{0} ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . All methods share training and evaluation settings, except for method-specific hyperparameters. Three controls on Qwen3-8B math retain centering and alter one component of the full method. No gate sets g t = 1 g_{t}=1 while retaining the gate-mean normalization rule. Shuffled gate permutes gates among valid response prefixes within a batch, retaining each prefix’s candidate weights and centered endpoint signal. No normalization fixes κ B = 1 \kappa_{B}=1 while retaining the positive-cosine gate. Appendix E gives definitions and invariants of the shuffle control. We separately vary the math Waypoint over teacher RL steps 500, 600, and 700 on Qwen3-8B in Appendix F .

sections.heading: 5 Results and Analysis
sections.text: We compare transfer performance across math and code at three student scales (Section 5.1 ). We examine learning trajectories and performance relative to the Final teacher on Qwen3-8B math (Section 5.2 ). We assess the roles of temporal gating, gate assignment, and mean normalization through ablations (Section 5.3 ).

sections.heading: Code.
sections.text: Waypoint-OPD improves over Direct-OPD by 2.66, 1.52, and 1.19 percentage points on average for Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, with gains in all 15 code comparisons. OPD 2 achieves higher scores on 14B LCB v5 and on 30B-A3B MBPP and MBPP+, while Waypoint-OPD retains the highest average for each student (Appendix D ). The 14B and 30B-A3B students also surpass the Final teacher’s 55.37 average by 2.45 and 2.17 points, respectively, each scoring higher on four of the five code evaluations.

sections.heading: Interpreting the endpoint comparison.
sections.text: The gains over Direct-OPD show that Waypoint-OPD improves transfer performance across both domains and all three student scales. OPD and OPD 2 provide complementary comparisons with Final-teacher imitation and selective distillation based on advantage sign agreement, respectively.

sections.heading: Consistent gains across training checkpoints.
sections.text: Waypoint-OPD delivers consistent gains over Direct-OPD across both benchmarks and training checkpoints. Excluding the shared initialization, it scores higher in 13 of the 15 benchmark–checkpoint comparisons, with two exceptions early in training. From step 60 onward, Waypoint-OPD leads on all three benchmarks at every recorded evaluation, showing that its advantage is sustained through the end of training. The step-100 gains are 4.17, 3.13, and 0.10 percentage points on AIME 2025, AIME 2026, and HMMT November 2025, respectively. These results show that gains extend beyond the selected checkpoint to sustained advantages during training.

sections.heading: Comparison with the Final teacher.
sections.text: The gray reference lines distinguish gains over endpoint transfer from performance relative to the teacher. On HMMT November 2025, Waypoint-OPD exceeds the Final teacher’s 40.83 at steps 60, 80, and 100, reaching 42.60 at step 60. On both AIME benchmarks, its recorded scores remain below the corresponding teacher reference. Improvements over Direct-OPD therefore coexist with different teacher–student orderings across benchmarks. The sustained HMMT advantage demonstrates that Waypoint-OPD can use the teacher’s policy shifts to achieve performance beyond the Final teacher’s score.

sections.heading: Removing the gate.
sections.text: On Qwen3-8B math, removing the gate lowers Avg. from 56.14 to 53.50, a decrease of 2.64 points, with lower scores on all seven benchmarks (Table 3 ). Retaining centering and normalization without consistency-dependent weighting therefore does not recover the full method’s gain. This comparison does not isolate the effect of centering.

sections.heading: Disrupting the gate–prefix association.
sections.text: Shuffling gates lowers Avg. to 51.20, which is 4.94 points below the full method and 2.30 below the ungated variant, with the same ordering on every benchmark. Random reassignment is thus more detrimental than removing the selective weighting in this setting, supporting the value of matching each gate to the prefix whose temporal agreement produced it.

sections.heading: Removing mean normalization.
sections.text: Fixing κ B = 1 \kappa_{B}=1 while retaining the positive-cosine gate lowers Avg. by 0.92 points to 55.22. Normalization improves six of seven benchmarks. The exception is HMMT February 2025 (34.79 without normalization versus 34.38 with it). The unnormalized variant still exceeds Direct-OPD by 1.26 points on average and on all seven benchmarks. Thus, the advantage persists without batch normalization, which provides an additional average benefit here. The remaining gain cannot be assigned entirely to gating because centering and other differences from Direct-OPD are also retained.

sections.heading: Ablation insights.
sections.text: These ablations support temporal weighting, its prefix assignment, and an incremental benefit from normalization in Qwen3-8B math. Their gaps are conditional on the retained components, not independent additive contributions. For a fixed rollout batch, shuffling preserves the gate distribution and κ B \kappa_{B} , while advantage and gradient norms depend additionally on the gate–signal pairing (Appendix E ). Supplementary diagnostics show stronger average gate attenuation in later batches, while mean-gate normalization does not fix the reward norm (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: On-policy distillation and policy-shift transfer.
sections.text: Knowledge distillation transfers teacher distributions or generated sequences ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Kim and Rush, 2016 ) , while on-policy variants supervise student-generated trajectories ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Complementary work refines divergence objectives and the use of teacher- and student-generated data ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) . Weak-to-strong generalization asks whether weaker supervision can elicit stronger capabilities ( Burns et al., 2024 ) . WSPO and proxy-tuning reuse a weak model’s adaptation contrast for training and decoding, respectively ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Within on-policy training, Direct-OPD transfers an RL-induced policy change through an endpoint log-ratio on student rollouts ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . W2S-OPD constructs a proxy teacher by adding a weak-model logit contrast to student base logits, then minimizes reverse KL on student rollouts. Its contrasts span RL checkpoints, model scales, and correct versus incorrect hints ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . OPRD uses a centered teacher–reference shift to amplify the component of a verifier-driven gradient along that direction ( Park et al., 2026 ) . Waypoint-OPD builds on Direct-OPD, weighting local endpoint signals by agreement between shifts before and after a Waypoint checkpoint.

sections.heading: Selective supervision in distillation.
sections.text: Teacher–student compatibility affects the utility of on-policy supervision ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Prune-OPD uses support overlap for suffix attenuation ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . EOPD uses teacher uncertainty in its entropy-dependent forward KL ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , while PW-OPSD uses token position in its reference-conditioned self-distillation ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . OPD 2 gates sampled-token updates by sign agreement between centered teacher–base and teacher–student advantages ( Heo et al., 2026 ) , whereas RG-OPD gates trajectories using agreement between verifier-derived advantages and teacher–student sequence log-likelihood gaps ( Akhondzadeh et al., 2026 ) . Waypoint-OPD uses different evidence: consecutive shifts in the teacher’s own RL trajectory over student-supported candidate actions. Their weighted directional agreement produces a prefix-level gate for the dense endpoint update, without verifier feedback during transfer. This agreement is a weighting criterion, not a guarantee of correctness.

sections.heading: Checkpoint selection and progressive distillation.
sections.text: A teacher’s final performance need not determine its teaching utility: early stopping and intermediate checkpoint selection can improve distillation ( Cho and Hariharan, 2019 ; Wang et al., 2022 ) . Pro-KD and progressive distillation use successive teacher checkpoints as targets or a curriculum ( Rezagholizadeh et al., 2022 ; Panigrahi et al., 2025 ) . Direct-OPD also studies RL checkpoint choice for transfer ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . For fixed Initial and Final endpoints, Waypoint measures directional consistency between the two shifts. It supplies neither an imitation target nor a curriculum. The centered Initial-to-Final shift remains the transferred object.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented Waypoint-OPD, which uses agreement between consecutive teacher shifts to transfer RL-induced policy changes. An intermediate Waypoint checkpoint reveals whether early and late changes in relative action preferences reinforce or oppose each other at student-generated prefixes. This information, unavailable from endpoint differences alone, determines the weight of the centered Initial-to-Final shift in the student’s on-policy objective. The method requires one additional frozen-teacher scoring pass and no verifier calls during transfer. Experiments on mathematical and code reasoning show gains over endpoint transfer across three Qwen3 student scales. Ablations on Qwen3-8B math support prefix-specific gate assignment and batch-scale normalization. These findings suggest that intermediate teacher checkpoints provide evidence for weighting local policy changes during student learning.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: We use generative AI tools for language polishing, assistance in clarifying mathematical derivations, and consistency checks of notation and exposition. These tools were not used for experimental design, implementation, or execution. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work.

sections.heading: Use of Human Annotations
sections.text: Human annotations are only used in methodological research at the beginning of the work, to assist in analyzing the feasibility of the proposed solution. Annotators consented to the use of data for research purposes. We ensure that the privacy of all annotators is protected throughout the annotation process, and all of them are adequately paid according to local standards. Human annotations are not applied during the evaluation of our method.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.text: In this paper, all datasets are obtained from official sources. The datasets adopted have been anonymized and do not contain offensive information. However, we cannot guarantee that the datasets do not contain socially harmful or toxic language.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: The transfer objective is specified in Section 3 , with supporting derivations and signal properties in Appendix A and pseudocode and optimization details in Appendix B . Section 4.1 describes the teacher checkpoints, student models, training and evaluation data, evaluation metrics, and student checkpoint selection. Appendix C reports hyperparameters, hardware, and evaluation settings. Baselines and controls are described in Section 4.2 , with precise definitions of the gate and normalization ablations in Appendix E and the Waypoint-position ablation setup in Appendix F . Per-benchmark results and domain averages appear in Tables 1 and 7 , and gate and normalization ablation results appear in Table 3 .

However, this endpoint policy shift cannot reveal whether local action preferences evolved consistently during teacher training. The same endpoint shift can result from early and late shifts that reinforce or partially cancel each other. We investigate whether agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts can guide selective transfer. We introduce Waypoint-guided On-Policy Distillation (Waypoint-OPD), which uses an intermediate teacher checkpoint from the same RL run to compare early and late shifts in relative action preferences at student-visited prefixes. We gate the endpoint shift according to the directional agreement between the early and late shifts, suppressing it when they point in opposing directions. Compared with endpoint-only transfer, our method requires only one additional frozen-teacher scoring pass. Using RL-trained Qwen3-4B teachers, we evaluate our method with Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B as student models in mathematical and code reasoning. In all six domain–student settings, Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest domain-average score among the compared distillation methods. Ablations with the Qwen3-8B student show that removing or shuffling gates reduces mathematical reasoning performance. These results support the use of directional agreement between early and late teacher policy shifts to weight the endpoint shift during student training. Our code is available at https://github.com/hhhbxloveai/WaypointOPD . Figure 1: Mathematical reasoning across three student models. mean@32 accuracy (%), averaged over seven benchmarks. Waypoint-OPD improves over Direct-OPD by 2.18, 1.59, and 1.89 percentage points, respectively. Teacher scores are from the Final Qwen3-4B checkpoint. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning can improve language-model instruction following using rewards learned from human preferences ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and mathematical and code reasoning using verifiable rewards ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . The latter requires repeated generation, verification, and optimization of on-policy responses. Reusing a teacher’s RL improvements offers a way to share this training effort across target models. This raises the question: which local changes in the teacher’s policy should guide a student on its own generated trajectories? Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) trains the student to match the teacher’s token distributions on student-generated prefixes ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Its supervision remains tied to the teacher’s absolute policy and capability limitations. On-Policy Delta Distillation ( OPD 2 ) uses the change between a reasoning-tuned teacher and its base model, retaining token-level signals when the centered change agrees in sign with the centered standard distillation signal ( Heo et al., 2026 ) . Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) focuses on RL-induced improvements. It uses the log-probability ratio between pre-RL and post-RL teacher checkpoints as a dense implicit reward on student-generated states, transferring the teacher’s policy change without matching its absolute distribution ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . Both methods extract changes from a pair of teacher models, but neither directly measures whether consecutive changes during teacher RL point in compatible directions. The Initial-to-Final log-probability ratio captures only the change between the teacher’s policies before and after RL training. The same endpoint signal can arise from early and late policy changes that point in similar or opposing directions. Endpoint-only transfer cannot distinguish these cases. We hypothesize that agreement between the early and late changes provides evidence for deciding how much weight to assign an endpoint shift at a student-generated prefix. Building on this hypothesis, we propose Waypoint-OPD, which uses agreement between consecutive teacher shifts to gate the endpoint transfer signal. We retain three checkpoints from the same teacher RL run: Initial before RL, Waypoint at an intermediate RL step, and Final at the end of RL. At each student-generated prefix, we select its top- k k most probable next-token candidates. Over these candidates, we compare how the teacher’s relative preferences change from Initial to Waypoint and from Waypoint to Final. Their agreement gates the centered Initial-to-Final signal, retaining aligned changes and suppressing reversals. Waypoint thus supplies evidence for weighting the endpoint shift, which remains the transferred signal. Relative to endpoint-only transfer, this requires one additional frozen teacher scoring pass, with no new teacher training or verifier calls during student transfer. Our contributions are: • Temporal agreement as a criterion for selective transfer. We use the Waypoint checkpoint to assess temporal agreement at student-generated prefixes, revealing directional information unavailable from the endpoint pair alone. • Waypoint-guided gating of endpoint signals. We develop Waypoint-OPD, a dense on-policy objective that uses this agreement to weight the endpoint signal at each student-generated prefix, with one additional frozen teacher scoring pass. • Higher average performance across domains and model sizes. We evaluate Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) on mathematics and code. Waypoint-OPD achieves the highest recorded domain average among the evaluated baselines in all six settings (Figure 1 and Tables 1 and 2 ). Ablations on Qwen3-8B mathematical reasoning support the value of temporal gating (Table 3 ). 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Problem setup and notation Let x ∼ 𝒟 x\sim\mathcal{D} be a prompt, y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) a response, and s t = ( x , y < t ) s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) the prefix at which a candidate token a a is scored. We measure the teacher’s RL-induced change relative to π 0 \pi_{0} and regularize student updates relative to student initialization π S \pi_{S} . Knowledge distillation transfers teacher distributions or generated sequences ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Kim and Rush, 2016 ) , while on-policy variants supervise student-generated trajectories ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Complementary work refines divergence objectives and the use of teacher- and student-generated data ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) . Weak-to-strong generalization asks whether weaker supervision can elicit stronger capabilities ( Burns et al., 2024 ) . WSPO and proxy-tuning reuse a weak model’s adaptation contrast for training and decoding, respectively ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Within on-policy training, Direct-OPD transfers an RL-induced policy change through an endpoint log-ratio on student rollouts ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . W2S-OPD constructs a proxy teacher by adding a weak-model logit contrast to student base logits, then minimizes reverse KL on student rollouts. Its contrasts span RL checkpoints, model scales, and correct versus incorrect hints ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . OPRD uses a centered teacher–reference shift to amplify the component of a verifier-driven gradient along that direction ( Park et al., 2026 ) . Waypoint-OPD builds on Direct-OPD, weighting local endpoint signals by agreement between shifts before and after a Waypoint checkpoint. Selective supervision in distillation. Teacher–student compatibility affects the utility of on-policy supervision ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Prune-OPD uses support overlap for suffix attenuation ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . EOPD uses teacher uncertainty in its entropy-dependent forward KL ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , while PW-OPSD uses token position in its reference-conditioned self-distillation ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . OPD 2 gates sampled-token updates by sign agreement between centered teacher–base and teacher–student advantages ( Heo et al., 2026 ) , whereas RG-OPD gates trajectories using agreement between verifier-derived advantages and teacher–student sequence log-likelihood gaps ( Akhondzadeh et al., 2026 ) . Waypoint-OPD uses different evidence: consecutive shifts in the teacher’s own RL trajectory over student-supported candidate actions. Their weighted directional agreement produces a prefix-level gate for the dense endpoint update, without verifier feedback during transfer. This agreement is a weighting criterion, not a guarantee of correctness. Checkpoint selection and progressive distillation. A teacher’s final performance need not determine its teaching utility: early stopping and intermediate checkpoint selection can improve distillation ( Cho and Hariharan, 2019 ; Wang et al., 2022 ) . Pro-KD and progressive distillation use successive teacher checkpoints as targets or a curriculum ( Rezagholizadeh et al., 2022 ; Panigrahi et al., 2025 ) . Direct-OPD also studies RL checkpoint choice for transfer ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . For fixed Initial and Final endpoints, Waypoint measures directional consistency between the two shifts. It supplies neither an imitation target nor a curriculum. The centered Initial-to-Final shift remains the transferred object. 7 Conclusion We presented Waypoint-OPD, which uses agreement between consecutive teacher shifts to transfer RL-induced policy changes. An intermediate Waypoint checkpoint reveals whether early and late changes in relative action preferences reinforce or oppose each other at student-generated prefixes. This information, unavailable from endpoint differences alone, determines the weight of the centered Initial-to-Final shift in the student’s on-policy objective. The method requires one additional frozen-teacher scoring pass and no verifier calls during transfer. Experiments on mathematical and code reasoning show gains over endpoint transfer across three Qwen3 student scales. Ablations on Qwen3-8B math support prefix-specific gate assignment and batch-scale normalization. These findings suggest that intermediate teacher checkpoints provide evidence for weighting local policy changes during student learning.
